{{< include ../../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

This page is a demonstration lab: it walks through the exercise of the course, Tasks 1 to 5, on a copy of R that runs inside the browser, but it fits no model. Every result on it was computed by the course pipeline with the code of the downloadable workspace, and the page reads it from small tables, so the page and the workspace give the same numbers. Each result sits beside the code of the workspace that produces it, shown as a block that does not run here. The facilitator uses the page on the shared screen to walk through the tasks, and if your machine fails on the day you can follow the tasks here and still send your two results to the class chart. Everyone taking the course works in the downloadable workspace described on the [Setup](../../setup.qmd) page, which fits every model live; to fit a model yourself, or to try a specification or a causal graph that this page does not hold, use the workspace.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## While the R engine loads

The R engine, four packages with their dependencies (about 7.5 MB) and the tables of the course (about 0.2 MB) download into your browser the first time you open this page, which can take up to a minute on a slow connection. Read Task 1 while they load. You will know that the page is ready when the first code cell switches from a loading spinner to a "Run Code" button.

Keep this tab open. Your work stays in this page until you refresh it – there is nothing to install, nothing to save to disk, and no account needed.
:::

```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Lab machinery: the specification menu, its validation, and the helpers of
# Tasks 4 and 5 – try_spec(), my_experiments(), submit_exploration(), prereg(),
# run_spec() and report_result(). The page fits nothing: the result of every
# specification is its row of data/spec_curve.csv, which the course pipeline
# fitted with the estimator of the workspace (R/spec_tools.R, a copy of
# R/trust/_tools.R), and data/menu_options.csv gives the reason for every
# option that is not on the curve. Both arrive with the page through its
# `resources:` list. The workspace fits the same specifications live and
# prints the same lines.

# ============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION – the class chart and the course site
# ============================================================================
# The results Form that submit_exploration() and report_result() pre-fill: its
# ID and the entry codes of its seven fields. They belong to the Form that the
# cases of the course share, set up for the EU-frames case; a Form of its own
# replaces them here and nowhere else. The word in .case_word follows the tag
# in every label, so that the chart of this case reads only its own rows.
.form_id <- "1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A"
.form_entry <- c(spec = "entry.832496914", b = "entry.1656311800", se = "entry.1337458262",
                 t = "entry.1940779437", df = "entry.1682711955", n = "entry.1586392724",
                 r = "entry.1660273001")
.case_word <- "trust"
.course_url <- "https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication"
# ============================================================================


# ---- The menu of the curve and the label of the class chart --------------------
# As R/trust/_tools.R defines them. Every combination of the options of
# SPEC_AXES is one specification of the curve (4 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 2 = 192).
SPEC_AXES <- list(
  outcome  = c("parliament", "politicians", "legal", "index"),
  controls = c("none", "demog", "outlook", "paper"),
  weights  = c("none", "design", "population"),
  items    = c("complete", "available"),
  fe       = c("country_round", "country_and_round")
)

# The free-text label that carries a specification to the class chart.
spec_line <- function(outcome, controls, weights, items, fe) {
  sprintf("outcome=%s controls=%s weights=%s items=%s fe=%s", outcome, controls, weights, items, fe)
}


# ---- The menu --------------------------------------------------------------------
# The twelve decisions in the order of the menu, each with the options that
# the curve keeps. The five decisions of SPEC_AXES keep two or more options,
# which multiply to the 192 specifications; on the other seven the curve keeps
# one. Every other option is a row of data/menu_options.csv, whose reason the
# helpers print when it is asked for.
.menu <- list(
  # Level 1 – Estimands
  outcome   = SPEC_AXES$outcome,
  controls  = SPEC_AXES$controls,
  weights   = SPEC_AXES$weights,
  sample    = "paper",
  # Level 2 – Measurement
  concern   = "index",
  items     = SPEC_AXES$items,
  education = "five",
  votes     = "cabinet",
  missing   = "listwise",
  # Level 3 – Estimation
  fe        = SPEC_AXES$fe,
  errors    = "country",
  scale     = "points"
)
.level_titles <- c(estimand    = "Level 1 – Estimands",
                   measurement = "Level 2 – Measurement",
                   estimation  = "Level 3 – Estimation")


# ---- The shipped files -----------------------------------------------------------
# Each file is read once and cached. The base reader adds nothing to the
# download of the page, and reads empty cells as NA, as readr does.
.cache <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.read_once <- function(name, path) {
  if (is.null(.cache[[name]])) {
    if (!file.exists(path))
      stop(sprintf("%s is missing – the page loads it through its resources list. Reload the page.",
                   path), call. = FALSE)
    assign(name, utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8", # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
                                 na.strings = c("", "NA")),
           envir = .cache)
  }
  .cache[[name]]
}
.curve   <- function() .read_once("curve", "data/spec_curve.csv")
.options <- function() .read_once("options", "data/menu_options.csv")


# ---- Pages of the course site ----------------------------------------------------
.pages <- c(
  "cases/trust/index.qmd"       = "Case study",
  "cases/trust/menu.qmd"        = "Specification menu",
  "cases/trust/map.qmd"         = "Decision map",
  "cases/trust/multiverse.qmd"  = "Multiverse",
  "companion/dags.qmd"          = "Causal graphs and adjustment sets",
  "companion/measurement.qmd"   = "The items behind the scales",
  "companion/weighting.qmd"     = "Weights",
  "companion/missingness.qmd"   = "Missing answers",
  "companion/stats-methods.qmd" = "The statistical methods behind the course",
  "companion/multiverse.qmd"    = "The multiverse and its critics")
.page_ref <- function(path) {
  title <- if (path %in% names(.pages)) .pages[[path]] else path
  sprintf("%s, %s/%s", title, .course_url, sub("\\.qmd$", ".html", path))
}
.or_list <- function(x) {
  q <- paste0("\"", x, "\"")
  if (length(q) == 1) q else paste(paste(q[-length(q)], collapse = ", "), "or", q[length(q)])
}


# ---- Validation ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two entry points into the same rules. .validate() takes a named list, which
# is how try_spec() supplies its arguments; .check_choices() reads the twelve
# my_* choices of the preregistration cell. An option that is not on the
# curve stops with the reason from menu_options.csv, the page of the course
# site that teaches it, and the options that stay on the curve. The rows are
# found with datawizard::data_match(), which takes the values to match as a
# list and so works inside a function; remove_na = FALSE, because with its
# default it drops incomplete rows before matching and can return the wrong
# rows.
.on_menu <- function(axis, v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v) && v %in% .menu[[axis]]

.refuse <- function(axis, v, as_args) {
  shown <- if (as_args) axis else paste0("my_", axis)
  keep  <- .menu[[axis]]
  map   <- paste0("  Every decision and its options: ", .page_ref("cases/trust/map.qmd"))
  if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || is.na(v))
    stop(sprintf("%s needs one option in quotes, for example %s = \"%s\".", shown, shown, keep[1]),
         call. = FALSE)
  opts <- .options()
  row  <- datawizard::data_match(opts, list(axis = axis, option = v), remove_na = FALSE)
  off  <- datawizard::data_match(opts, list(axis = axis, on_curve = FALSE), remove_na = FALSE)$option
  msg <- if (nrow(row) == 1) c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" (%s) is not on the curve of %d specifications, so it has no result here.",
            shown, v, row$label, nrow(.curve())),
    paste0("  Why: ", row$reason),
    paste0("  Where it is taught: ", .page_ref(row$taught_on)),
    map,
    sprintf("  To stay on the curve, choose %s = %s.", shown, .or_list(keep))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not an option on the menu.", shown, v),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s.", paste(keep, collapse = " | ")),
    if (length(off) > 0)
      sprintf("  Off the curve, refused with the reason why: %s.", paste(off, collapse = " | ")),
    map
  )
  stop(paste(msg, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)
}

.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {
  bad <- purrr::discard(names(.menu), \(a) .on_menu(a, ch[[a]]))
  if (length(bad) > 0) .refuse(bad[1], ch[[bad[1]]], as_args)
  ch[names(.menu)]
}

# The choices are looked up from the frame of this function outwards, which
# reaches the session in which the preregistration cell was run.
.check_choices <- function() {
  need <- paste0("my_", names(.menu))
  ch <- mget(need, envir = environment(), inherits = TRUE, ifnotfound = list(NULL))
  missing <- need[purrr::map_lgl(ch, is.null)]
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice in the preregistration cell and run it first.", call. = FALSE)
  .validate(stats::setNames(ch, names(.menu)))
}


# ---- The result of a specification ------------------------------------------------
# The row of data/spec_curve.csv for the five decisions that vary on the curve:
# the estimate with its 95% interval and test under errors clustered by
# country (t on 15 df), the conventional test, the counts and the partial r,
# as the estimator of the workspace computes them; and its place among the 192.
.result <- function(ch) {
  curve <- .curve()
  stored <- datawizard::data_match(curve, ch[c("outcome", "controls", "weights", "items", "fe")],
                                   remove_na = FALSE)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1)
    stop("This specification has no row in data/spec_curve.csv; reload the page.", call. = FALSE)
  c(as.list(stored), list(larger = sum(curve$b > stored$b + 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(curve)))
}


# ---- The printout ----------------------------------------------------------------
.fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 1e-4) "< 0.0001" else sprintf("= %s", format(signif(p, 2), scientific = FALSE))
.fmt_n <- function(n) format(round(n), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)

.class_line <- function(res) {
  above <- res$b > 0
  sig   <- res$p < 0.05
  if (above && sig) "above zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim"
  else if (above) "above zero, but not significant at 5%"
  else if (sig) "below zero and significant at 5%, against the direction of the claim"
  else "below zero and not significant at 5%"
}

.print_result <- function(ch, res, lead = NULL) {
  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    paste0("  ", spec_line(ch$outcome, ch$controls, ch$weights, ch$items, ch$fe)),
    sprintf("  Estimate: %.4f points of distrust per point of concern, 95%% interval %.3f to %.3f",
            res$b, res$ci_low, res$ci_high),
    sprintf("  Test: t = %.2f on %d df, p %s (errors clustered by country, %d countries)",
            res$stat, round(res$df), .fmt_p(res$p), res$n_clusters),
    sprintf("        conventional errors, which treat respondents as independent: t = %.2f on %s df",
            res$t_conv, .fmt_n(res$df_conv)),
    sprintf("  n = %s respondents in %d country-rounds, partial r = %.3f (the conversion rule of Multi100)",
            .fmt_n(res$n), res$n_country_rounds, res$r),
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %d of the %d specifications have a larger estimate",
            res$larger, res$n_curve)))
  invisible(res)
}


# ---- Task 4: the exploratory helpers -----------------------------------------------
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("log", NULL, envir = .tried)
assign("last", NULL, envir = .tried)

# The first five arguments are the decisions on which the curve keeps more
# than one option; the other seven are fixed on the curve, and asking for any
# other option of theirs prints the reason why it is not on the curve.
try_spec <- function(outcome = "parliament", controls = "paper", weights = "none",
                     items = "complete", fe = "country_round", sample = "paper",
                     concern = "index", education = "five", votes = "cabinet",
                     missing = "listwise", errors = "country", scale = "points") {
  ch <- .validate(list(outcome = outcome, controls = controls, weights = weights,
                       sample = sample, concern = concern, items = items,
                       education = education, votes = votes, missing = missing,
                       fe = fe, errors = errors, scale = scale), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  row <- data.frame(ch, b = res$b, ci_low = res$ci_low, ci_high = res$ci_high,  # r-style: keep – data.frame() spreads the list of choices into columns
                    t = res$stat, p = res$p, n = res$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", if (is.null(.tried$log)) row else datawizard::data_merge(.tried$log, row, join = "bind"),
         envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}

# The running log of everything that try_spec() has looked up. Only the
# decisions that varied are shown; the others are those of the reference
# specification. The datawizard verbs here name only columns of the log, which
# they can see from inside a function.
my_experiments <- function() {
  d <- .tried$log
  if (is.null(d)) {
    writeLines("Nothing tried yet – call try_spec() at least once.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  varied <- purrr::keep(names(.menu), \(a) length(unique(d[[a]])) > 1)
  show <- d |>
    datawizard::data_modify(estimate = round(b, 4),
                            interval = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", ci_low, ci_high),
                            t = round(t, 2)) |>
    datawizard::data_select(c(varied, "estimate", "interval", "t", "n"))
  writeLines(sprintf("Specifications you have tried (%d), estimates in points of distrust per point of concern:\n",
                     nrow(d)))
  # wide enough for all five varied decisions on one line
  old_width <- options(width = max(getOption("width"), 120))
  on.exit(options(old_width))
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines(sprintf("\nEstimates from %.4f to %.4f  |  above zero and significant at 5%%: %d of %d",
                     min(d$b), max(d$b), sum(d$b > 0 & d$p < 0.05), nrow(d)))
  invisible(show)
}

submit_exploration <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  if (is.null(.tried$last))
    stop("Nothing to submit – call try_spec() first, ending with the specification you want on the chart.",
         call. = FALSE)
  .submit(.tried$last$ch, .tried$last$res, "explore",
          "Your exploratory submission (the last specification you tried):", nickname)
}


# ---- Task 5: the declared helpers --------------------------------------------------
# prereg() prints the cell and returns it, so that run_spec() can check that
# the cell has not changed since. The estimand statement is assembled from
# the phrase column of menu_options.csv, in the order that its codebook sets;
# the row of each choice is found in the order of the menu.
prereg <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  rows <- purrr::imap(ch, \(option, axis) datawizard::data_match(.options(), list(axis = axis, option = option),
                                                                 remove_na = FALSE)) |>
    purrr::list_rbind() |>
    datawizard::data_modify(line = sprintf("    %-20s : %-17s (%s)", decision, option, label))
  block <- purrr::imap(.level_titles, \(title, lv) c(paste0("  ", title), rows$line[rows$level == lv])) |>
    unlist(use.names = FALSE)
  ph <- stats::setNames(rows$phrase, rows$axis)
  statement <- c(
    sprintf("%s%s, %s, the change in %s that goes with one more point of %s (%s), %s (%s, %s, %s).",
            toupper(substr(ph[["sample"]], 1, 1)), substring(ph[["sample"]], 2), ph[["weights"]],
            ph[["outcome"]], ph[["concern"]], ph[["items"]], ph[["controls"]],
            ph[["education"]], ph[["votes"]], ph[["missing"]]),
    sprintf("Estimated by %s, tested %s and reported %s.", ph[["fe"]], ph[["errors"]], ph[["scale"]]))
  writeLines(c(
    "DECLARED – your preregistered specification, fixed before it is fitted:",
    "",
    block,
    "",
    "  The estimand statement",
    strwrap(statement, width = 78, indent = 4, exdent = 4),
    "",
    "run_spec() and report_result() read these choices from here. Copied into",
    "your notes, this cell is your preregistration."))
  invisible(structure(list(choices = ch), class = "trust_prereg"))
}

run_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "trust_prereg"))
    stop("Pass the object that prereg() returned: my_spec <- prereg(), then run_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (!identical(spec$choices, .check_choices()))
    stop("The preregistration cell has changed since prereg() returned this object. Run the whole cell again, then run_spec(my_spec).",
         call. = FALSE)
  .print_result(spec$choices, .result(spec$choices),
                "Your preregistered specification, as the course pipeline fitted it:")
}

report_result <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  .submit(ch, .result(ch), "declared",
          "Your declared submission (straight from your preregistration):", nickname)
}


# ---- Submission tags ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Both submissions of a participant carry one short tag inside the spec label,
# "explore: [amber-otter-42] trust …", so that the participant can find their
# own marks on the class chart. The same functions sit in R/spec_tools.R of
# the workspace, which keeps the tag in a file; here it lasts for the browser
# session, and a nickname passed to either submission function sets it or
# brings it back after a reload.
.tag_words <- list(
  adj  = c("amber", "azure", "bright", "calm", "coral", "crisp", "dusky", "early",
           "fair", "gentle", "golden", "hazel", "ivory", "jade", "keen", "lively",
           "lunar", "misty", "noble", "olive", "pale", "quiet", "rapid", "rosy",
           "russet", "silver", "snowy", "solar", "sunny", "swift", "velvet", "vivid"),
  noun = c("otter", "heron", "lynx", "badger", "finch", "hare", "ibex", "kestrel",
           "lark", "marten", "newt", "owl", "puffin", "quail", "raven", "seal",
           "stoat", "tern", "vole", "wren", "bison", "crane", "dove", "egret",
           "fox", "gecko", "koala", "lemur", "moose", "panda", "robin", "swan")
)
.tag_env <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("tag", NULL, envir = .tag_env)

# A fresh tag, drawn without touching the random-number stream of the session.
.new_tag <- function() {
  had_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
  if (had_seed) old_seed <- get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
  on.exit(if (had_seed) assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = globalenv())
          else rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()))
  set.seed(as.integer((as.numeric(Sys.time()) * 1000) %% 1e9) + Sys.getpid() %% 1e5)
  paste(sample(.tag_words$adj, 1), sample(.tag_words$noun, 1), sample(10:99, 1), sep = "-")
}

# A nickname reduced to lower-case ASCII letters, digits and single hyphens,
# at most 24 characters – the only form that the class chart parses.
.clean_tag <- function(x) {
  # iconv on Windows turns these into "?": the Romanian comma-below letters and the eszett
  x <- gsub("ß", "ss", chartr("ȘșȚț", "SsTt", trimws(as.character(x)[1])))
  ascii <- suppressWarnings(iconv(x, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"))
  if (!is.na(ascii)) x <- ascii
  x <- gsub("^-+|-+$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x)))
  x <- gsub("-+$", "", substr(x, 1, 24))
  if (is.na(x) || !nzchar(x))
    stop("A nickname needs at least one letter or digit, for example nickname = \"blue-heron\".",
         call. = FALSE)
  x
}

# The tag of this session: the nickname if one is given, otherwise the tag
# already drawn, otherwise a fresh one. Returns the tag and the one it replaced.
.class_tag <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  stored <- .tag_env$tag
  tag <- if (!is.null(nickname)) .clean_tag(nickname) else if (!is.null(stored)) stored else .new_tag()
  assign("tag", tag, envir = .tag_env)
  list(tag = tag, replaced = if (!is.null(stored) && !identical(tag, stored)) stored)
}

# One submission, used by both phases. The phase, the tag and the word of the
# case are prefixed to the free-text spec label, which carries the five
# decisions that vary on the curve. The estimate and its standard error are
# sent in points of distrust per point of concern, the t of the errors
# clustered by country with its 15 df, and r by the rule of Multi100 from the
# conventional t, as the r column of spec_curve.csv holds it.
.submit <- function(ch, res, phase, lead, nickname = NULL) {
  tg <- .class_tag(nickname)
  spec_label <- paste0(phase, ": [", tg$tag, "] ", .case_word, " ",
                       spec_line(ch$outcome, ch$controls, ch$weights, ch$items, ch$fe))
  value <- c(spec = spec_label, b = sprintf("%.5f", res$b), se = sprintf("%.5f", res$se),
             t = sprintf("%.3f", res$stat), df = as.character(round(res$df)),
             n = as.character(res$n), r = sprintf("%.3f", res$r))
  query <- purrr::imap_chr(.form_entry, \(entry, k)
    paste0(entry, "=", utils::URLencode(value[[k]], reserved = TRUE))) |>
    paste(collapse = "&")
  url <- sprintf("https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/%s/viewform?usp=pp_url&%s", .form_id, query)

  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    "",
    paste("  spec:", spec_label),
    sprintf("  b = %s | se = %s | t = %s | df = %s | n = %d | r = %s",
            value[["b"]], value[["se"]], value[["t"]], value[["df"]], res$n, value[["r"]]),
    "  (b and se in points of distrust per point of concern; t with errors clustered by country)",
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    "",
    "Open the link below (or copy the URL) – the form opens with every field",
    "pre-filled; just press Send.",
    "",
    url))
  if (requireNamespace("htmltools", quietly = TRUE))
    print(htmltools::tags$p(htmltools::tags$a(href = url, target = "_blank",
                                              "Open the pre-filled form in a new tab")))
  writeLines(c(
    "",
    sprintf("Your marks on the class chart carry the tag %s%s.", tg$tag,
            if (!is.null(tg$replaced)) sprintf(" (it replaces %s)", tg$replaced) else ""),
    sprintf("Look for it on the Multiverse page, %s/cases/trust/multiverse.html.", .course_url),
    "Both of your submissions share it while this page stays open; after a reload,",
    sprintf("bring it back with nickname = \"%s\". To choose your own, pass a", tg$tag),
    "nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public."))
  invisible(list(spec = spec_label, tag = tg$tag, b = res$b, se = res$se, statistic = res$stat,
                 df = res$df, n = res$n, r = res$r, url = url))
}
```

Five analysts reanalysed a claim of the immigration-and-trust case [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope] for the Multi100 project [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]; you are analyst no. 6. The claim is that "... concerns about the effect of immigration on the national community have a(n) \[reducing\] impact on trust in politics", in the words of the original author (OA) as the SCORE programme selected them. The [exercise overview](exercise.qmd) sets out the five tasks, and the [case study](index.qmd) the original study, Multi100 and the five reanalyses.

The five tasks take you from a setup check to two marks on the live class chart, one submitted while you explore the menu in Task 4 and one that you declare in your preregistration in Task 5 before you look up its result. The cells of this page read the results that the course pipeline computed on the ESS extract with the estimator of the workspace, so each answer comes at once; the blocks marked "In the workspace" hold the code that computes the same results in the workspace.

## Task 1 – The setup check {#task-1-setup}

## Warm-up – the three Rs {#warm-up}

The warm-up settles the vocabulary before you touch any data. Three of the four scenarios below describe one of our three Rs – reproducibility, robustness, replicability – and the fourth describes something else. Read all four, then label each one in the code cell.

***Scenario 1:*** A team rebuilds the variables of the paper from the ESS files, fits its three-level model, and gets 0.178 points of distrust per point of concern against the published 0.17. It analyses 69,522 respondents rather than the 110,732 of the paper, because it leaves out everyone with a missing answer on any variable of the model. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though the sample does not match.

***Scenario 2:*** An analyst takes the file that the team built, fits the model in Stata instead of R, and measures concern with the single item on whether immigrants make the country a worse or a better place to live. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team fits the model to the next round of the ESS, fielded in 2010 in 13 of the 16 countries, and finds 0.183. Their conclusion is that the original finding has \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** Another researcher asks whether concern about refugees goes with distrust of politics among citizens of Central and Eastern Europe, using another survey ten years later, and finds the same pattern. The researcher concludes that the original finding \_\_\_\_\_\_ to other societies and another measure.

Fill in the gaps in the code cell below and run it to print your answers back.

```{webr}
#| exercise: vocab
#| code-overflow: wrap
writeLines(c(
  "Scenario 1: This is an example of ______.",
  "Scenario 2: Is this a case of ______ or ______?",
  "Scenario 3: The original finding has ______.",
  "Scenario 4: The original finding ______ to other societies and another measure."
))
```

:::: {.solution exercise="vocab"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Answers

1.  **reproducibility** – a reproduction from the source data, which SCORE scored as reproducing the coefficient approximately but not the sample.
2.  a grey area. Rerunning an analysis of the same file in different software is still **reproducibility**, but the single item in place of the index of three is an analytic choice, which makes it a test of **robustness**.
3.  **replicated** (replicability) – the same question asked of independent new data.
4.  **generalises** (generalisability) – the odd one out, with new societies, new data and a new measure at once.
:::
::::

## Task 2 – The data {#task-2-data}

The **ESS extract** (`trust_ess.csv`) holds one row per respondent: every respondent of the 16 countries in rounds 1–4 of the European Social Survey (ESS). It is adapted from the ESS files of those rounds and shared under their licence, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The downloadable workspace loads it as `ess` and computes everything below from it; this page does not download it (about 10 MB) and reads the results instead, which the course pipeline computed with the same code (`R/trust/06_displays.R`; the tables have a [codebook](data/lab_tables_codebook.md)). Each trust item is turned round, so that every distrust column runs from 0 (complete trust) to 10 (no trust at all), and each immigration item too, so that 10 is the answer most concerned about immigration. The [codebook](data/trust_ess_codebook.md) describes every column.

In the workspace, the counts of respondents, countries and country-rounds, and of the sample of the paper (citizens who do not belong to an ethnic minority):

``` r
ess |>
  datawizard::data_summary(respondents    = n(),
                           countries      = dplyr::n_distinct(cntry),
                           country_rounds = dplyr::n_distinct(paste(cntry, essround)),
                           paper_sample   = sum(citizen %in% 1 & minority %in% 0))
```

On this page, run the cell below to read the same counts:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# The counts that the code above gives, written by the course pipeline and
# printed as datawizard prints its summaries
utils::read.csv("data/lab_counts.csv") |>  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
  insight::export_table()
```

You should find **120,080 respondents** in **16 countries** and **60 country-rounds**, and **110,732** in the sample of the paper, the count that it reports in every table. The paper leaves out non-citizens and members of ethnic minorities, because its argument concerns members of the national community who believe that community to be under threat.

The concern of the claim is measured by three items. A scale built from several items measures an attitude with less error than any single item, provided that the items move together. Cronbach's alpha says how far they do: it runs from 0 (the items are unrelated) to 1 (they move in lockstep), and values above about 0.7 are usually taken as good enough for a scale. In the workspace:

``` r
# The sample of the paper, with concern as the mean of the three items. A
# respondent who skipped any item has no score (NA): min_valid = 3 asks for
# all three answers.
paper <- ess |>
  datawizard::data_filter(citizen == 1, minority == 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(concern = datawizard::row_means(dplyr::pick(imm_econ, imm_culture, imm_place),
                                                min_valid = 3))

# Cronbach's alpha of the three items, on the respondents who answered all three
paper |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("imm_econ", "imm_culture", "imm_place")) |>
  stats::na.omit() |>
  performance::cronbachs_alpha()

# The mean distrust of the three institutions, and the mean concern
paper |>
  datawizard::describe_distribution(select = c("distrust_parl", "distrust_pol", "distrust_legal", "concern")) |>
  datawizard::print_md()
```

On this page:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Cronbach's alpha of the three items, the pooled row ("all") of the
# reliability table that the pipeline writes with performance::cronbachs_alpha()
reliability <- utils::read.csv("data/display_reliability.csv")  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
datawizard::data_filter(reliability, scale == "concern", cntry == "all")$alpha

# The distributions of the three outcomes and of concern, from
# datawizard::describe_distribution()
utils::read.csv("data/lab_distribution.csv") |>  # r-style: keep – as above
  insight::export_table(digits = 2)
```

Alpha comes out at **0.84**, close to the average of 0.83 that the paper reports. The mean distrust is **5.08** for parliament, **6.06** for politicians and **4.45** for the legal system, within 0.01 of the means that the paper prints in its Table 1. Now the countries. In the workspace, the mean concern and the mean distrust of parliament in each country, with the correlation of the two within it:

``` r
by_country <- paper |>
  datawizard::data_summary(r_within      = stats::cor(concern, distrust_parl, use = "complete.obs"),
                           concern       = mean(concern, na.rm = TRUE),
                           distrust_parl = mean(distrust_parl, na.rm = TRUE),
                           by = "cntry")
```

On this page, the 16 rows of `by_country` come from the pipeline, and the rest of the cell is the code of the workspace:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
by_country <- utils::read.csv("data/lab_countries.csv")  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download

# The correlation across countries, and its range within them
stats::cor(by_country$concern, by_country$distrust_parl)
range(by_country$r_within)

# The 16 country means, drawn with tinyplot: the regression line across the
# countries in grey, then the code of each country at its means
tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(distrust_parl ~ concern, data = by_country, type = tinyplot::type_lm(se = FALSE),
                   col = "grey70", lwd = 1.5,
                   xlim = range(by_country$concern), ylim = range(by_country$distrust_parl),
                   xlab = "Mean concern about immigration (0–10)", ylab = "Mean distrust of parliament (0–10)")
tinyplot::tinyplot(distrust_parl ~ concern, data = by_country,
                   type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = by_country$cntry, font = 2, xpd = TRUE),
                   col = "#0e3b6a", add = TRUE)
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

Across the 16 countries, the correlation of mean concern with mean distrust of parliament is **0.68**: where citizens worry more about immigration, they distrust their parliament more. Greece is the most concerned country, and Portugal distrusts its parliament most. Within each country the correlation is much weaker, from about **0.17** in Southern Europe to **0.38** in Norway. The claim is about respondents, not countries, and countries differ in their history of immigration, their politics and the performance of their governments, any of which can move both averages at once. So every specification of the curve compares respondents of the same country, surveyed in the same round.

## Task 2, continued – The estimand and the graph {#task-2-estimand-and-graph}

Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template that you can adapt [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand]:

> The **unit-specific quantity** is, for each respondent, the difference between the distrust of parliament that they would report if they were one point more concerned about immigration and the distrust that they report now. The **target population** is the citizens of the 16 Western European countries in 2002–2009 who do not belong to an ethnic minority.

The catch is that nobody observes the same respondent at two levels of concern: the ESS interviewed different people in each round, so the data can only compare respondents who differ in concern. Whether that comparison answers the question depends on what else differs between them.

A causal graph sets this out. A graph of this kind is a diagram of what causes what: variables are nodes, arrows run from cause to effect, and the rules for reading the graph say which paths between concern and distrust are open, given what the comparison holds constant. The graph below is written in ordinary R, one arrow per string, each written the way it is drawn, so that `"pessimism -> concern"` is the arrow from a pessimistic outlook to concern about immigration. Background characteristics (age, sex, education, income), a general pessimism and ideology can each shape both concern and distrust, which makes them possible confounders. A vote for a far-right party and the verdict on public services and the economy may follow from concern, from distrust, or from both. The arrow from concern to distrust, which is the effect that the claim is about, is switched off with a `#`.

```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Graph machinery for Task 2. make_dag() builds the graph from its arrows and
# plot_dag() draws it with tinyplot. adjustmentSets(), isAdjustmentSet() and
# paths() print the answers of dagitty, the R package that the workspace uses,
# in the form in which dagitty prints them, from data/dag_answers.csv:
# R/trust/07_dag_answers.R in the course repository computes them with dagitty
# for every graph to which the graph cell below leads – the arrow of the claim
# off, on or reversed, each with either swap – and for the adjustment sets of
# the menu. dagitty itself cannot run on this page, because its graph
# algorithms need a JavaScript engine that a browser grants only to a page
# served with cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP), and the course
# site does not send them. Another graph, or another question, goes to dagitty
# in the downloadable workspace. The table arrives with the page through its
# `resources:` list; the rows are found with datawizard::data_match(), which
# works inside a function, with remove_na = FALSE, because with its default it
# drops incomplete rows before matching and can return the wrong rows.
.dag_answers <- utils::read.csv("data/dag_answers.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE,  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
                                na.strings = "NA", colClasses = c(latent = "character"))
.dag_elsewhere <- c(
  "This page holds the answers that dagitty gives to the questions of Task 2, for the graph",
  "of the cell with the arrow of the claim off, on or reversed, each with either swap, and for",
  "the adjustment sets of the menu. For another graph or another question, use the",
  "downloadable workspace, where R/dag_starter.R builds the graph and dagitty answers",
  "whatever you ask of it.")

# Where each node sits in the figure, with y counted upwards: concern on the
# left, distrust on the right, the possible common causes above the line
# between them and the possible consequences below it. A node without a
# position here is drawn on a row below the graph.
.dag_xy <- list(concern = c(0, 0), distrust = c(4, 0), background = c(2, 2.4),
                pessimism = c(0.7, 1.5), ideology = c(3.3, 1.5),
                far_right = c(2, -1.1), services = c(2, -2.1))

# A graph from arrows written "cause -> effect", one per string. The named
# arguments come last, so that switching off the last arrow with a # never
# leaves a comma dangling. The arrows, sorted, are the key under which
# data/dag_answers.csv holds the answers for the graph.
make_dag <- function(..., exposure = "concern", outcome = "distrust", latent = character(0)) {
  arrows <- c(...)
  ends <- purrr::map(arrows, \(a) {
    e <- trimws(strsplit(a, "->", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
    if (length(e) < 2 || !all(nzchar(e)) || grepl("<-", a, fixed = TRUE))
      stop(sprintf("Write each arrow as \"cause -> effect\", for example \"pessimism -> concern\"; \"%s\" is not one.",
                   a), call. = FALSE)
    e
  })
  from <- unlist(purrr::map(ends, \(e) e[-length(e)]))
  to <- unlist(purrr::map(ends, \(e) e[-1]))
  drawn <- paste(from, to, sep = " -> ")
  structure(list(edges = list(from = from[!duplicated(drawn)], to = to[!duplicated(drawn)]),
                 nodes = unique(c(exposure, outcome, from, to)),
                 exposure = exposure, outcome = outcome, latent = latent,
                 key = paste(sort(unique(drawn), method = "radix"), collapse = "; ")),
            class = "simple_dag")
}

# The minimal adjustment sets of the exposure on the outcome, for the total or
# the direct effect, as dagitty::adjustmentSets() returns them, read from the
# table
adjustmentSets <- function(x, exposure = x$exposure, outcome = x$outcome, type = "minimal",
                           effect = "total", ...) {
  rows <- datawizard::data_match(.dag_answers,
                                 list(call = "adjustmentSets", arrows = x$key,
                                      exposure = paste(exposure, collapse = ", "),
                                      outcome = paste(outcome, collapse = ", "),
                                      latent = paste(sort(x$latent, method = "radix"), collapse = ", "),
                                      effect = effect),
                                 remove_na = FALSE)
  if (nrow(rows) == 0 || !identical(type, "minimal")) {
    writeLines(.dag_elsewhere)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  structure(strsplit(rows$answer[rows$item > 0], ", ", fixed = TRUE), class = "simple_dag_sets")
}

# As dagitty prints adjustment sets: one set per line, the empty set as {},
# and nothing at all when no set closes every path that it must
print.simple_dag_sets <- function(x, ...) {
  purrr::walk(x, \(z) writeLines(if (length(z) == 0) " {}" else
    strwrap(paste("{ ", paste(z, collapse = ", "), " }\n"), exdent = 2)))
  invisible(x)
}

# Registered rather than left in the session: these cells do not evaluate in
# the global environment, so plain S3 dispatch would not find the method.
registerS3method("print", "simple_dag_sets", print.simple_dag_sets)

# Whether a set of variables closes every path that it must for the total
# effect, as dagitty::isAdjustmentSet() answers, read from the table
isAdjustmentSet <- function(x, Z, exposure = x$exposure, outcome = x$outcome, ...) {
  rows <- datawizard::data_match(.dag_answers,
                                 list(call = "isAdjustmentSet", arrows = x$key,
                                      exposure = paste(exposure, collapse = ", "),
                                      outcome = paste(outcome, collapse = ", "),
                                      latent = paste(sort(x$latent, method = "radix"), collapse = ", "),
                                      Z = paste(sort(unique(as.character(unlist(Z))), method = "radix"),
                                                collapse = ", ")),
                                 remove_na = FALSE)
  if (nrow(rows) != 1) {
    writeLines(.dag_elsewhere)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  as.logical(rows$answer)
}

# The paths between the exposure and the outcome, each with its arrows, and
# whether it is open given the conditioning set Z, as dagitty::paths() returns
# them, read from the table
paths <- function(x, from = x$exposure, to = x$outcome, Z = list(), limit = 100, directed = FALSE) {
  rows <- datawizard::data_match(.dag_answers,
                                 list(call = "paths", arrows = x$key,
                                      exposure = paste(from, collapse = ", "),
                                      outcome = paste(to, collapse = ", "),
                                      latent = paste(sort(x$latent, method = "radix"), collapse = ", "),
                                      Z = paste(sort(unique(as.character(unlist(Z))), method = "radix"),
                                                collapse = ", ")),
                                 remove_na = FALSE)
  if (nrow(rows) == 0 || !isFALSE(directed)) {
    writeLines(.dag_elsewhere)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  list(paths = rows$answer, open = rows$open)
}

# The figure. Colour marks the exposure and the outcome. Each arrow stops at
# the edge of the box of its target, which is sized from the length of the name.
plot_dag <- function(d) {
  x <- purrr::map_dbl(d$nodes, \(v) if (v %in% names(.dag_xy)) .dag_xy[[v]][1] else NA_real_)
  y <- purrr::map_dbl(d$nodes, \(v) if (v %in% names(.dag_xy)) .dag_xy[[v]][2] else NA_real_)
  unplaced <- is.na(x)
  x <- replace(x, unplaced, 1.2 * (cumsum(unplaced)[unplaced] - 1))
  y <- replace(y, unplaced, -3)
  half_w <- 0.06 + 0.032 * nchar(d$nodes)
  role <- factor(datawizard::recode_into(d$nodes %in% d$exposure ~ "exposure",
                                         d$nodes %in% d$outcome ~ "outcome",
                                         d$nodes %in% d$latent ~ "unobserved",
                                         default = "observed"),
                 levels = c("exposure", "outcome", "observed", "unobserved"))
  # how far along a unit vector (ux, uy) the edge of a box of half-width w lies
  to_edge <- \(ux, uy, w) pmin(w / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), 0.15 / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9))
  tail <- match(d$edges$from, d$nodes)
  head <- match(d$edges$to, d$nodes)
  len <- sqrt((x[head] - x[tail])^2 + (y[head] - y[tail])^2)
  ux <- (x[head] - x[tail]) / len
  uy <- (y[head] - y[tail]) / len
  s0 <- to_edge(ux, uy, half_w[tail])
  s1 <- to_edge(ux, uy, half_w[head]) + 0.04

  # the boxes, coloured by role; tinyplot has no type for arrows, so they go
  # on the same canvas through graphics::arrows(); then the names, white on
  # the coloured boxes and dark on the pale one
  tinyplot::tinyplot(xmin = x - half_w, xmax = x + half_w, ymin = y - 0.13, ymax = y + 0.13,
                     by = role, type = "rect",
                     palette = c("#1b6ca8", "#d1495b", "grey45", "grey88"), fill = "by",
                     legend = list("bottom!", title = NULL), axes = FALSE, frame.plot = FALSE,
                     xlab = NA, ylab = NA,
                     xlim = range(x) + c(-0.45, 0.45), ylim = range(y) + c(-0.3, 0.3),
                     grid = FALSE, theme = "minimal")
  graphics::arrows(x[tail] + s0 * ux, y[tail] + s0 * uy, x[head] - s1 * ux, y[head] - s1 * uy,
                   length = 0.1, angle = 20, col = "grey40", lwd = 1.5)
  tinyplot::tinyplot(x = x, y = y, by = role,
                     type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = d$nodes, font = 2),
                     palette = c("white", "white", "white", "grey25"), cex = 0.8, add = TRUE)
}
```

`make_dag()` builds the graph and `plot_dag()` draws it. `adjustmentSets()`, `isAdjustmentSet()` and `paths()` print the answers of dagitty, the R package that the downloadable workspace uses for the same questions, in the form in which dagitty prints them. The course pipeline computed those answers ([codebook](data/dag_answers_codebook.md)) for every graph that the cell below offers: the arrow of the claim off, on or reversed, each with either of the two swaps, and for the four adjustment sets of the menu. For any other graph, the workspace runs dagitty itself:

``` r
source("R/dag_starter.R")
plot_dag(dag)
dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag)
paper_set <- c("background", "pessimism", "ideology", "far_right", "services")
dagitty::paths(dag)
dagitty::paths(dag, Z = paper_set)
dagitty::isAdjustmentSet(dag, paper_set)
```

Now build the graph and put three questions to it. What has to be held constant to estimate the effect of concern on distrust? Which paths between the two are open before anything is held constant? And which are open once the controls of the paper are held constant, the background, pessimism and ideology together with the far-right vote and the verdict on services?

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
my_dag <- make_dag(
  # Background, pessimism and ideology can each shape both attitudes.
  "background -> concern",
  "background -> distrust",
  "pessimism -> concern",
  "pessimism -> distrust",
  "ideology -> concern",
  "ideology -> distrust",
  # A far-right vote can follow from concern and from distrust; if you think
  # instead that the vote deepens distrust, swap the second line for the third.
  "concern -> far_right",
  "distrust -> far_right",
  # "far_right -> distrust",
  # So can the verdict on public services; if you think instead that poor
  # services feed distrust, swap the second line for the third.
  "concern -> services",
  "distrust -> services",
  # "services -> distrust",

  # The effect that the claim is about: take the # off if you believe it.
  # "concern -> distrust",

  exposure = "concern", outcome = "distrust"
)

paper_set <- c("background", "pessimism", "ideology", "far_right", "services")
adjustmentSets(my_dag)              # r-style: keep – the function of this page, which prints the answer of dagitty
paths(my_dag, Z = paper_set)        # r-style: keep – as above
isAdjustmentSet(my_dag, paper_set)  # r-style: keep – as above
plot_dag(my_dag)
```

`adjustmentSets()` returns `{ background, ideology, pessimism }`. Three paths connect concern and distrust through their common causes, and holding those three constant closes them. The two paths through the far-right vote and the verdict on services are closed already, because each runs into a common effect of concern and distrust (a collider). Holding the controls of the paper constant closes the first three paths but opens these two, and `isAdjustmentSet()` answers `FALSE`: comparing respondents who voted alike and judge the services alike makes concern and distrust go together even in this graph, in which concern has no effect on distrust at all.

Now take the `#` off the arrow `"concern -> distrust"` and run the cell again. Then try the two swaps that the cell offers, one at a time, and finally replace the arrow of the claim with `"distrust -> concern"`. Answer three questions for your own notes: whether the adjustment set changes once the arrow of the claim is on; what the far-right vote and the verdict on services become after the swaps, and what holding them constant then estimates; and whether any set of controls can separate the two directions of the arrow.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers

1.  The set stays `{ background, ideology, pessimism }`. The arrow of the claim is the effect itself, not a path to be blocked, and the controls of the paper still open the two collider paths.
2.  After the swaps they are mediators: part of the effect of concern runs through them. Holding them constant removes that part and leaves what the graph calls the direct effect, which `adjustmentSets(my_dag, effect = "direct")` shows, so the controls of the paper then answer a narrower question than the claim.
3.  No. With `"distrust -> concern"`, the path `concern <- distrust` stays open whatever is held constant, and `adjustmentSets()` finds no set and prints nothing, so a comparison of respondents at one point in time cannot tell the two directions apart. One Multi100 analyst raised this reverse direction, and the paper says that an analysis with instrumental variables confirmed its own direction, but does not report it.

The four adjustment sets of the menu follow the graph: no controls (`"none"`), the background (`"demog"`), the background with pessimism and ideology (`"outlook"`), and those with the verdicts on the economy and public services and the two vote controls, the set of the paper (`"paper"`). The adjustment set is the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and whatever you conclude here belongs in field 4 of your preregistration in Task 5.
:::

## Task 3 – The reproduction {#task-3-reproduction}

This is the **reproducibility** check. All five Multi100 analysts worked from one file, which a SCORE reproduction had built from the ESS files of rounds 1–4 with the variables of the paper already coded (osf.io/e48gd). Analyst 6U3LL fitted the model of Table 3 of the paper to it, without the unemployment rate of each country: a three-level model with random intercepts for countries and for country-rounds, fitted in R with the lmerTest package, which builds on lme4. Multi100 recorded **t = 46.625** on 72,733 respondents, and the coefficient behind it, which the log of the analyst prints, is 0.191.

The workspace reproduces that value: it downloads the file from the OSF once and fits the model with lme4. A page in a browser cannot download the file, because the OSF serves it through a redirect that does not give a page on another website permission to read it, a rule that every browser enforces (cross-origin resource sharing), and the course cannot host a copy of its own, because the file holds person-level survey data. In the workspace, the reproduction is this code:

``` r
have_srd <- fetch_multi100()

srd <- read.csv(.multi100$path)  # r-style: keep – the reader in the script of the analyst

m_6u3ll <- lme4::lmer(
  trstprl_r ~ im_conc + happy_r + stflife_r + sclmeet_r + distrust + stfeco_r + hincfel +
    stfhlth_r + stfedu_r + winner + far_right + lrscale + hhinc_std + agea + edulvla + female +
    far_right_share + spr_estat + factor(round) + long_im_his + wgi + GDP +
    (1 | country_round) + (1 | cntry),
  data = srd)

stats::nobs(m_6u3ll)
lme4::ngrps(m_6u3ll)
# the coefficient of concern, read with parameters; the t to three decimals
coefs_6u3ll <- parameters::model_parameters(m_6u3ll, effects = "fixed", keep = "^im_conc$")
coefs_6u3ll
round(coefs_6u3ll$t, 3)
```

The course pipeline ran the same model on the same file (`R/trust/04_reference_marks.R`), and the cell below reads what it found: the respondents and groups of the fit, then the coefficient of concern with its standard error, *t* and degrees of freedom, as `parameters` reads them.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
reproduction <- utils::read.csv("data/lab_reproduction.csv")  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
reproduction |>
  datawizard::data_filter(id == "6U3LL") |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("n", "country_rounds", "countries", "b", "se", "t", "df"))
round(datawizard::data_filter(reproduction, id == "6U3LL")$t, 3)
```

The model gives **t = 46.625** on **72,733 respondents**, in 57 country-rounds of 16 countries, with a coefficient of 0.191: the value on record for analyst 6U3LL, reproduced from the file of the analysts. Multi100 also recorded 72,700 degrees of freedom, which come from the lmerTest package that the analyst loaded: it adds an approximation of the degrees of freedom to the same *t*, which lme4 reports without them.

What do the random intercepts contribute? The workspace fits the same individual-level model with an intercept for every country-round instead (fixed effects), which absorb the country-level variables, constant within a country-round:

``` r
m_fe <- fixest::feols(
  trstprl_r ~ im_conc + happy_r + stflife_r + sclmeet_r + distrust + stfeco_r + hincfel +
    stfhlth_r + stfedu_r + winner + far_right + lrscale + hhinc_std + agea + edulvla + female |
    country_round,
  data = srd, vcov = "iid")
parameters::model_parameters(m_fe, keep = "^im_conc$")
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
utils::read.csv("data/lab_reproduction.csv") |>  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
  datawizard::data_filter(id == "6U3LL_fe") |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("n", "country_rounds", "b", "se", "t", "df"))
```

The coefficient barely moves: 0.1914 with an intercept for every country-round as with the random intercepts, and *t* = 46.60 against 46.62. With hundreds of respondents in every country-round, random and fixed intercepts give almost the same answer. The course data come next. The specification of the course closest to the model of 6U3LL is distrust of parliament, the controls of the paper, and an intercept for every country-round, with the scales built as the file of the analysts builds them. The file of the analysts builds each scale from the items that a respondent answered, which is one of the two options of the decision `items`. The cell below is an exercise: replace the blank (`______`) with that option, then press "Run Code". If you get stuck, open the hint below; the solution has the full code.

```{webr}
#| exercise: analogue
# The specification of the course closest to the model of 6U3LL: its row of
# the curve, which the course pipeline fitted on the course data
curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv")  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
datawizard::data_filter(curve, outcome == "parliament", controls == "paper", weights == "none",
                        items == "______", fe == "country_round") |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("b", "t_conv", "n", "n_country_rounds"))
```

:::: {.hint exercise="analogue"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint – the rule for unanswered items

The two options of `items` are `"complete"` (a scale counts only for respondents who answered every item) and `"available"` (it averages the items that were answered).
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="analogue"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution

``` r
curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv")  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
datawizard::data_filter(curve, outcome == "parliament", controls == "paper", weights == "none",
                        items == "available", fe == "country_round") |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("b", "t_conv", "n", "n_country_rounds"))
```

You should get a coefficient of **0.174** on **72,620 respondents** in 57 country-rounds, with a conventional *t* of 41.7, against 0.191 and 46.625 on the file of the analysts. In the workspace, `fit_spec(ess, items = "available")[, c("b", "t_conv", "n", "n_country_rounds")]` fits the same specification live and prints the same numbers.
:::
::::

The gap of 0.017 does not come from the model. On the file of the analysts, fixed and random intercepts give almost exactly the same coefficient, so the gap lies in the two files. They code several variables differently, among them the vote for a party in government (the file of the analysts counts only voters for the party that won the last election) and the far-right vote.

*Optional extension.* The SCORE reproduction osf.io/jp7tr rebuilt the data of the paper from the ESS files and published a coefficient of 0.1780 on 69,522 respondents. It read the integrated files of the four rounds, which lack the Italian round 2. In the workspace, leave that country-round out of the course data and fit the reference specification:

``` r
without_it2 <- datawizard::data_filter(ess, !(cntry == "IT" & essround == 2))
fit_spec(without_it2)[, c("b", "se", "t_conv", "n", "n_country_rounds")]
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
utils::read.csv("data/lab_reproduction.csv") |>  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
  datawizard::data_filter(id == "course_no_it2") |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("b", "se", "t_conv", "n", "country_rounds"))
```

The fit keeps exactly the 69,522 respondents of that reproduction and gives 0.1772, within 0.001 of its published 0.1780, without any multilevel model. The [case study](index.qmd) traces the small gap that remains to the coding of the vote controls.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproduction and the five analysts

In the workspace, everyone reproduces the recorded value exactly, because everyone runs the same code on the same file. This is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish.

The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for this claim, and all five concluded that their results were evidence for it, in the direction that the paper reports. Their coefficients still differ by a factor of two, from 0.115 to 0.235 points of distrust per point of concern, largely because one analyst measured concern with a single item and another held constant a much shorter list of controls. One of them also doubted the direction of the effect: "one could argue for an at least partially reverse direction of the effect, given that there is ample evidence that trust in authorities impacts on attitudinal variables". The [case study](index.qmd) sets out what each analyst chose.
:::

## Task 4 – The menu {#task-4-menu}

This task is **exploratory**. You try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing in this task is preregistered; the preregistration comes in Task 5.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and every argument defaults to the reference specification, the one closest to the model of the paper: distrust of parliament, the controls of the paper, no weights, every item of a scale answered, an intercept for every country-round. So changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays as it was. On this page every call reads the row of the curve that the course pipeline fitted for that specification; in the workspace, the same call fits it live and prints the same lines.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Nothing changed – the reference specification.
try_spec()
```

The printout gives the estimate in points of distrust per point of concern with its 95% interval, the *t* test with errors clustered by country (the rule that classes every point of the curve, on 15 degrees of freedom for 16 countries), the *t* of conventional errors for comparison, the number of respondents and country-rounds analysed, the partial *r* by the conversion rule of Multi100, the class of the result, and its place among the 192 specifications on the curve of the claim.

Each of the five calls below changes a single decision. The first three change the question that is being asked of the data, the fourth changes how the scales are measured, and the last changes only how the same question is estimated. Run them and compare the results.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(outcome  = "politicians")        # distrust of politicians instead of parliament
try_spec(controls = "none")               # no controls: the claim as SCORE selected it
try_spec(weights  = "population")         # each country counted by its adult population
try_spec(items    = "available")          # scales averaged over the answered items
try_spec(fe       = "country_and_round")  # country intercepts and a shift for each round
```

The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, so trying one is part of the exercise. The helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve and names the page of the course that teaches it, and the [decision map](map.qmd) sets out every decision and its options on one page. Run the cell, then edit it to try others, such as `controls = "paper_gov"`, `sample = "all_respondents"`, `fe = "random_intercepts"`, `errors = "conventional"` or `weights = "post"`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# An option that is not on the curve: the helper refuses it and says why.
try_spec(concern = "culture")
```

Then try your own combinations. The full set of arguments, each with the reference specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(
  # the five decisions on which the curve keeps more than one option
  outcome   = "parliament",     # parliament | politicians | legal | index
                                #     off the curve: parties | european_parliament
  controls  = "paper",          # none | demog | outlook | paper
                                #     off the curve: paper_no_unhappy | paper_gov | paper_macro
  weights   = "none",           # none | design | population
                                #     off the curve: post | post_population
  items     = "complete",       # complete | available
  fe        = "country_round",  # country_round | country_and_round
                                #     off the curve: random_intercepts | pooled
  # the seven decisions that are fixed on the curve
  sample    = "paper",          # paper      off the curve: all_respondents | all_countries
  concern   = "index",          # index      off the curve: economy | culture | place
  education = "five",           # five       off the curve: seven
  votes     = "cabinet",        # cabinet    off the curve: nonvoters_missing | largest_party
  missing   = "listwise",       # listwise   off the curve: imputation | as_published
  errors    = "country",        # country    off the curve: country_round | conventional | cr2
  scale     = "points"          # points     off the curve: maximum_effect | standardised | r
)
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to view the small multiverse that you have just built. It shows only the decisions that you varied, so the differences are easy to read:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so that it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live [Multiverse]({{< var cases.trust.live-results-url >}}) chart as an open circle, labelled **exploratory**, and marked with the tag that the cell prints, such as `amber-otter-42`. The tag is how you find your own marks on the chart, and your declared result in Task 5 carries the same one. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exploratory and declared

Because you chose this specification after finding out what several specifications do, it lacks the guarantee that comes with a choice declared in a preregistration before its result is known: no one can rule out that it was chosen *because* of its result. This is something that we almost never know about published papers, unless their analysis was preregistered and every departure from the preregistration documented. In this course exploration is a natural step, and you also practise preregistering the analysis that you choose, so you submit twice, once here and once in Task 5.
:::

## Task 5 – The preregistration {#task-5-preregistration}

Preregistration means setting out your choice in a plan **before** you know what it does, which stops you from quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. On this page the plan is the preregistration cell below, and it binds mechanically as well: the session remembers the choices that you declare in that cell, and `run_spec()` and `report_result()` read them from there.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## A shortened preregistration

*Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

Make one choice on each decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), complete the dotted lines, then run the cell. The four decisions at Level 1 fix the question that you are asking, the five at Level 2 fix how it is measured, and the three at Level 3 fix how it is estimated. The curve of 192 specifications keeps two or more options on five of these decisions and a single option on the other seven. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: trust_ess.csv (120,080 respondents of
#    ESS rounds 1-4, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); I know that the reference specification
#    gives 0.175, and what my exploration in Task 4 showed.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each decision. An option that is
#    not on the curve of 192 stops prereg() with the reason why.

# Level 1 – Estimands (each of these changes what is being estimated)
my_outcome   <- "parliament"     # parliament | politicians | legal | index
my_controls  <- "paper"          # none | demog | outlook | paper
my_weights   <- "none"           # none | design | population
my_sample    <- "paper"          # paper   (citizens who do not belong to an ethnic minority)

# Level 2 – Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently)
my_concern   <- "index"          # index   (the mean of the three immigration items)
my_items     <- "complete"       # complete | available   (every item answered, or the answered ones)
my_education <- "five"           # five    (the five ISCED levels of the ESS)
my_votes     <- "cabinet"        # cabinet (votes for a party in government and for a far-right party)
my_missing   <- "listwise"       # listwise (respondents with a missing answer left out)

# Level 3 – Estimation (the same question and measures, another fit)
my_fe        <- "country_round"  # country_round | country_and_round
my_errors    <- "country"        # country (clustered by country, t on 15 df)
my_scale     <- "points"         # points  (points of distrust per point of concern)

# 4. Why this specification answers the claim, in one sentence grounded in
#    the causal graph of Task 2: .............................................
# 5. Supported if the estimate is above zero with p < .05 under errors
#    clustered by country; undermined if it is not significant or below
#    zero. I will report what I get.

my_spec <- prereg()   # checks every choice, prints your preregistration and keeps it
```

The cell above, copied into your notes, is your preregistration record.

## Task 5, continued – Look up, report and place {#task-5-fit-report}

This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you: together the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. `run_spec()` reads your declared specification from the curve, as the course pipeline fitted it, and prints the same lines as `try_spec()`; in the workspace it fits the specification live. It refuses to run if the preregistration cell has changed since `prereg()` read it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_spec)
```

The estimate is in points of distrust per point of concern, and a value above zero means that respondents who are more concerned about immigration distrust the institution more, the direction of the claim. Whether it is significant is decided by the test with errors clustered by country, and the line headed `Verdict:` says which of the four cases your result falls in.

Now send it to the class chart. The submission is built from your declaration, so there is nothing to fill in or transcribe. The cell prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; click it and press **Send**. Your mark joins the live [Multiverse]({{< var cases.trust.live-results-url >}}) chart within seconds, this time as a filled circle labelled **declared**, carrying the same tag as your exploratory result. If you have reloaded this page since Task 4, the session has forgotten that tag, so pass it back with `report_result(nickname = "your-tag")`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator, who adds your mark to the chart.

Finally, place your result on the curve of the claim: the 192 specifications that the menu keeps, ranked from the smallest estimate, coloured by the adjustment set, with yours ringed.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
spec_curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>  # r-style: keep – the base reader adds nothing to the download
  datawizard::data_arrange("b") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n(),
                          adjustment = factor(controls, levels = c("none", "demog", "outlook", "paper"),
                                              labels = c("none", "demographics", "outlook and ideology",
                                                         "controls of the paper")))
# Yours: the row of the five choices of the preregistration cell
mine <- datawizard::data_match(spec_curve, list(outcome = my_outcome, controls = my_controls,
                                                weights = my_weights, items = my_items, fe = my_fe),
                               remove_na = FALSE)

tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b ~ rank | adjustment, data = spec_curve, pch = 16,
                   palette = c("#b3cde3", "#6497c8", "#2166ac", "#08306b"),
                   legend = list("right!", title = "Controls"),
                   ylim = c(0, max(spec_curve$b)),
                   xlab = "The 192 specifications, from the smallest estimate",
                   ylab = "Points of distrust per point of concern")
tinyplot::tinyplot(b ~ rank, data = spec_curve, type = tinyplot::type_hline(h = 0), col = "grey60", add = TRUE)
# your specification, ringed; clim keeps a single ring at the size of cex
tinyplot::tinyplot(b ~ rank, data = mine, type = tinyplot::type_points(clim = c(3, 3)),
                   pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2.5, col = "#8b1538", add = TRUE)
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

All 192 estimates lie above zero, from 0.117 to 0.326 points of distrust per point of concern, and every one of them is significant at 5% with errors clustered by country (*t* from 11.3 to 21.6 on 15 df). The four bands are the four adjustment sets. The mean estimate is 0.290 without controls, 0.286 with the demographic controls, 0.214 with outlook and ideology, and 0.151 with the controls of the paper. The outcome moves the estimate by up to 0.055, and the weights, the rule for unanswered items and the intercepts each by less than 0.02. Within these data the claim holds under every choice on the menu; how large the association is depends above all on what is held constant, which is the question that the graph of Task 2 answers. The [Multiverse]({{< var cases.trust.live-results-url >}}) page sets the class submissions beside this curve.

If you want a second declared specification, edit the preregistration cell, rerun it, then rerun `run_spec(my_spec)`. The chart will still label it declared, so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so wherever you write about the result.

## Taking it home

This page keeps nothing once you refresh it, and it fits nothing, so work you want to keep, and every model you want to fit yourself, belongs in the downloadable workspace. Putting that work under version control and publishing the rendered report is the natural next step. The [Git and GitHub module](../../companion/git-github.qmd) of the companion curriculum explains it click by click.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## The downloadable workspace

The exercise on this page, Tasks 1 to 5, also exists in the downloadable workspace, the folder that you open in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), edit and render offline, and in which everyone taking the course works. There every result of this page is computed live: the ESS extract is loaded, every specification of the menu is fitted when you ask for it, dagitty answers any graph, and the reproduction of Task 3 downloads the file of the analysts and fits the model. The folder also holds the reproduction as a script, and a GitHub Actions workflow that renders the report and publishes it to GitHub Pages once the folder is pushed to a GitHub repository whose Pages source is set to GitHub Actions. The folder is maintained in the [`replication-lab-trust`]({{< var cases.trust.template-repo >}}) repository, and it is yours to reuse.
:::
